checklist.title: Verify Trust Boundary Integrity: Does validate_header (SG-005) properly reject blocks with header.number < 1?
checklist.test_procedure: 1. Identify the validate_header function in SG-005 that handles block header validation. 2. Trace all P2P entry points where block headers are received from external peers. 3. Verify that the validation explicitly checks header.number >= 1 before processing. 4. Attempt to submit a block with header.number = 0 via P2P and verify it is rejected with appropriate error. 5. Attempt to submit a block with negative header.number values (if applicable to the data type) and verify rejection. 6. Check for any code paths that might bypass this validation when processing blocks from peers. 7. Verify the error response does not leak sensitive information about internal state.
checklist.notes: Source: SG-005/INV-001. This is a boundary property at trust boundary tb-005. Genesis block has number 0, so all subsequent blocks must have number >= 1. A malicious peer could attempt to submit invalid blocks with header.number < 1 to exploit validation gaps. Pre-condition ensures blocks entering through P2P are properly validated before further processing.

checklist.title: Verify Internal Logic: Is the block number >= 1 invariant consistently enforced across all block processing paths?
checklist.test_procedure: 1. Identify all internal functions that process or reference block numbers after initial validation. 2. Verify that no internal code path assumes block.number can be 0 for non-genesis blocks. 3. Check state transition logic to ensure block number monotonically increases. 4. Review any caching or storage mechanisms that handle block numbers. 5. Verify that block number comparisons use correct operators (>= 1, not > 0) to handle edge cases. 6. Check for any integer underflow scenarios when decrementing block numbers.
checklist.notes: Source: SG-005/INV-001. Supporting check for the boundary property. Ensures that internal logic correctly handles the block number >= 1 invariant after boundary validation. Attempts to falsify by finding any path where block.number < 1 could be processed.

checklist.title: Verify Trust Boundary Integrity: Does validate_header (SG-005) enforce strictly increasing block timestamps (header.timestamp > parent_header.timestamp)?
checklist.test_procedure: 1. Identify the validate_header function in SG-005 that handles block header validation at the P2P trust boundary. 2. Trace all code paths where block timestamps are compared against parent timestamps. 3. Verify that the comparison uses strict inequality (>) and NOT non-strict (>=). 4. Attempt to submit a block via P2P with timestamp EQUAL to parent timestamp and verify rejection. 5. Attempt to submit a block via P2P with timestamp LESS than parent timestamp and verify rejection. 6. Attempt to submit a block with timestamp exactly 1 unit greater than parent and verify acceptance. 7. Test edge cases: (a) timestamp overflow scenarios, (b) maximum uint64 timestamp values, (c) timestamp at epoch boundaries, (d) very large time gaps between blocks. 8. Verify that error responses for invalid timestamps do not leak internal state information. 9. Check for any bypass paths where timestamp validation could be skipped for certain block types or sources.
attack_vectors: Malicious peer submitting headers with non-increasing timestamps to cause consensus divergence
Time manipulation attacks to influence block ordering or slot assignment
Replay attacks using headers with timestamps equal to existing blocks
Timestamp stagnation attacks to stall chain progress
checklist.notes: Source: SG-005/INV-002, Trust Boundary: tb-005. Block timestamp validation is critical for maintaining chain integrity and proper block ordering. This invariant ensures temporal ordering of the blockchain is preserved. A malicious actor on the P2P network can craft headers with invalid timestamps. Failure to enforce strict inequality could enable timestamp manipulation attacks affecting consensus, block ordering, or replay attacks. Elevated to High severity due to boundary exposure via P2P and potential consensus impact.
